label: Displacement Interpolation
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 113 through 162 and introduces McCann's displacement interpolation, the path that moves mass continuously along optimal transport rays. Stress at the outset that this construction turns the static Monge-Kantorovich problem into a dynamic one and supplies the geodesics of Wasserstein space, which organize the rest of the book.

label: From Static Plan to Moving Mass
notes: Recall that the previous chapters solved for an optimal coupling between two fixed measures. Here we ask the dynamic question: how does mass travel between them in time? Emphasize that the optimal plan already contains the answer, because each unit of mass simply follows the straight ray joining its source to its destination at constant speed.

label: McCann's Definition
notes: Define displacement interpolation as the pushforward of the source measure by the partial transport map. Walk through how at time zero we recover the source, at time one the target, and in between a genuinely new measure. Clarify that this is a one-parameter family of measures, not a curve in any finite-dimensional parameter space.

label: The Interpolation Formula
notes: Present the central formula in both map and plan form. For an optimal map the interpolant pushes the source forward by the convex combination of identity and map. With a plan we push the optimal coupling forward by the time-dependent point. Stress that the quadratic cost forces straight-line motion, so the geodesic is explicit.

label: Wasserstein Geodesics
notes: State the key theorem: displacement interpolants are exactly the constant-speed geodesics of the metric space of probability measures with the quadratic Wasserstein distance. Explain that the distance between endpoints is additive along the path and that speed equals the Wasserstein distance, which is what constant-speed geodesic means here.

label: Constant Speed and the Metric
notes: Make the constant-speed property quantitative: the Wasserstein distance from the source to the time-t measure grows linearly as t times the total distance. Demonstrate with the triangle-equality picture that the path is a true geodesic and not merely a continuous interpolation, since intermediate distances add exactly.

label: Displacement vs Linear Interpolation
notes: This is the conceptual heart of the chapter. Contrast displacement interpolation, which slides a bump bodily across the domain, with the linear interpolation of densities, which fades one bump out while another grows in. Point out that the linear interpolant develops two peaks and is not a geodesic, while displacement keeps a single travelling bump.

label: The Benamou-Brenier Action
notes: Introduce the dynamic formulation: among all curves of measures joining the endpoints and obeying the continuity equation, the geodesic is the one minimizing the kinetic action. Explain that this recasts the Wasserstein distance as a least-action principle, which is what makes the fluid-mechanical and Riemannian pictures of the space possible.

label: Continuity Equation and Velocity
notes: Derive the velocity field that transports the interpolant. The pair density-velocity solves the continuity equation, conserving mass at every instant. Emphasize that for the geodesic the velocity field is a gradient and is constant along each particle trajectory, which is the Eulerian shadow of straight-line Lagrangian motion.

label: Manifolds and Lagrangian Action
notes: Generalize beyond Euclidean space: on a Riemannian manifold mass moves along minimizing geodesics instead of straight segments, and the cost becomes a general Lagrangian action. Stress that displacement interpolation still produces Wasserstein geodesics and that this abstraction is what later connects optimal transport to Ricci curvature.

label: Computational Lab
notes: Walk through the notebook's discrete experiment. We solve a finite Monge-Kantorovich plan, then slide each unit of mass along its ray to build snapshots of the interpolation. The invariants checked are total mass one at every time and exact endpoint matching, which are the computational footprints of the geodesic property.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Summarize the three pillars: the explicit interpolation formula, the constant-speed geodesic theorem, and the Benamou-Brenier least-action characterization. Preview that treating Wasserstein space as a length space with these geodesics is the gateway to displacement convexity, gradient flows, and curvature bounds in the chapters that follow.
